summary: Defines a framework for extending Designated Forwarder election in Ethernet VPN. The DF is the provider edge router that sends broadcast, unknown unicast, and multicast traffic to a multihomed customer device. It defines an alternative to the default algorithm and a way to influence the result using attachment circuit state. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8584 improves how Ethernet VPN routers choose which router forwards broadcast traffic to a multihomed customer segment. It adds a fairer selection algorithm, an option to exclude routers whose attachment circuits are down, and rules for how routers agree on the procedure.

questions: what is a designated forwarder in evpn
subtitle: How Ethernet VPN routers agree which router forwards traffic for a multihomed segment.

tldr.problem: The default EVPN Designated Forwarder algorithm can distribute VLANs unevenly, remap many VLANs when a PE joins or leaves, and fail to notice when an attachment circuit cannot forward.
tldr.mechanism: A DF Election Extended Community lets PEs agree on an algorithm and capabilities. RFC 8584 defines Highest Random Weight selection, attachment-circuit-aware candidate filtering and a finite state machine.
tldr.outcome: If every PE on the segment agrees, it uses the selected procedure; if not, all use the RFC 7432 default. RFC 8584 updates RFC 7432 and is updated by RFC 9722 and RFC 9785.

today: RFC 8584 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7432. It has been updated by RFC 9722 and RFC 9785.

sections.title: The Designated Forwarder Role
sections.content:
An Ethernet VPN may connect one customer device to several provider edge routers on the same Ethernet Segment. For a given broadcast domain, one router is the Designated Forwarder (DF), responsible for sending broadcast, unknown-unicast and multicast traffic to that customer device. In single-active multihoming, the DF also sends unicast traffic.

Only one PE should forward BUM traffic to the segment, because Ethernet forwarding loops are severe and Ethernet has no TTL. All PEs attached to the segment therefore need to select the same DF.

The default service-carving algorithm from RFC 7432 uses the Ethernet Tag and number of PEs in a modulus calculation. RFC 8584 defines an extensible election framework that keeps the default as a fallback.
sections.plainLanguage: When several provider routers connect to one customer segment, they must agree which one forwards broadcast traffic. This RFC gives them more ways to make that choice while preserving a fallback for older routers.

sections.title: Problems with Modulus-Based Election
sections.content:
The default algorithm can distribute work unevenly when Ethernet Tags do not have a uniform distribution. For example, with two PEs and only even tags, the same PE can become DF for every VLAN.

When a PE joins or leaves, the number of candidates changes and the modulus may assign many VLANs to different PEs. This can cause unnecessary forwarding changes even for VLANs whose previous DF did not fail.

The algorithm also ignores the operational state of an individual attachment circuit. If a PE remains in the segment's candidate set while its circuit or bridge table is down, other PEs may continue to treat it as DF and traffic can be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The default calculation can assign most VLANs to one router and can change many assignments when one router joins or leaves. It can also select a router whose customer-facing circuit is not able to forward traffic.

sections.title: The DF Election State Machine
sections.content:
RFC 8584 specifies a finite state machine that EVPN implementations must follow. Its states are INIT, DF_WAIT, DF_CALC and DF_DONE. Events include ES_UP, ES_DOWN, VLAN_CHANGE, DF_TIMER, RCVD_ES, LOST_ES and CALCULATED.

When the segment comes up, the PE enters DF_WAIT, starts the wait timer and assumes it is not the DF. When the timer expires, it enters DF_CALC, rebuilds the candidate list and performs the election. After calculation it enters DF_DONE.

A changed, newly received or withdrawn ES route sends the PE from DF_DONE back to DF_CALC. ES_DOWN from any state stops the timer and returns the PE to INIT as a non-DF. The state machine does not protect against inconsistent local configuration among PEs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router waits for segment information, calculates the election and records the result. If the segment or its route information changes, the router runs the calculation again.

sections.title: Agreeing on Algorithms and Capabilities
sections.content:
A PE advertises its preferred DF procedure in a transitive DF Election Extended Community attached to its ES route. The community includes a five-bit DF Alg value and a two-octet capability bitmap. Algorithm 0 is the default modulus method, algorithm 1 is HRW, values 2 through 30 are unassigned and 31 is reserved for experiments.

Bitmap bit 1 indicates the AC-DF capability. A PE should attach the community to ES routes and must send it when it wants an algorithm other than the default or requires a capability.

Each PE compares the communities from all PEs on the segment. If they all match, it uses the indicated algorithm and capabilities. If any community is missing or differs, every PE uses the default algorithm with no capabilities. This keeps older RFC 7432 implementations compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: Each PE advertises one preferred algorithm and its capabilities. PEs use the new procedure only when every advertisement agrees; otherwise they use the default method.

sections.title: Highest Random Weight Selection
sections.content:
Highest Random Weight (HRW) calculates a weight for each candidate PE and Ethernet Tag, then selects the PE with the highest weight as DF. The PE with the next-highest weight is the Backup Designated Forwarder. Ties go to the PE with the numerically lowest IP address.

For EVPN, the weight uses the Ethernet Tag, Ethernet Segment Identifier (ESI) and PE IP address. The ESI adds information that reduces the chance that the same PE becomes DF for the same set of broadcast domains on multiple segments.

The RFC defines a deterministic weight calculation using a 31-bit digest of a 14-octet input: the four-octet Ethernet Tag followed by the ten-octet ESI. HRW can distribute work when tags are unevenly allocated, and a PE that is neither DF nor backup for a tag can leave without forcing those assignments to change.
sections.plainLanguage: HRW calculates a repeatable score for each PE and each Ethernet Tag. The highest score wins, the next-highest is the backup, and unrelated assignments can remain unchanged when another PE leaves.

sections.title: The AC-Influenced DF Capability
sections.content:
The AC-DF capability removes a PE from consideration when it cannot forward on the attachment circuit for a broadcast domain. A PE becomes a candidate only after the relevant Ethernet A-D per EVI route is received; withdrawal of that route or its Ethernet A-D per ES route removes the PE from the candidate set.

A local attachment-circuit change, or an update or withdrawal of either relevant route, triggers a new election. This lets the other PEs respond to a circuit or service failure even when the overall Ethernet Segment remains up.

For VLAN-aware bundle services, when every PE advertises AC-DF, election is performed per <ES, VLAN> rather than per <ES, VLAN Bundle>. Withdrawing one VLAN's route then removes that PE only for that VLAN.
sections.plainLanguage: AC-DF checks whether a PE can forward traffic on the relevant customer circuit before treating it as a candidate. A change in circuit or route status triggers a new election.

sections.title: Security and Agreement Requirements
sections.content:
The new procedures are intended to reduce uneven load, unnecessary service disruption and traffic black-holing. These conditions could also be deliberately created by a user able to change PE configuration.

The benefit depends on all PEs on an Ethernet Segment using consistent settings. If an attacker changes the configuration of one PE so its algorithm or capabilities differ, all PEs fall back to the default election and lose the new protections.

RFC 8584 extends RFC 7432, so the security considerations in RFC 7432 also apply. IANA assigns extended-community subtype 0x06, algorithm values and capability bits through their defined registries.
sections.plainLanguage: The improved election works only when every PE on the segment agrees. A conflicting configuration can force all PEs back to the default election.
